summary:
Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels, and Kedah stands under that national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya additionally maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those state offences reach Muslims only.

Kedah's own instrument is the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014). Sections 23 and 24 criminalise liwat (sodomy) and musahaqah (lesbian sex), each punishable by a fine of up to RM5,000, up to three years' imprisonment or up to six strokes of whipping, or any combination of those penalties. Section 26 criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, with a fine of up to RM1,000 or up to one year's imprisonment. Female cross-dressing is not an offence under the enactment.

Section 52 of the Kedah enactment adds a disposal measure: a woman convicted of musahaqah may be committed to an approved home for up to six months. This is state criminal law reaching Kedah residents who are Muslim, and it operates alongside the federal Penal Code rather than in place of it.

Enforcement in Kedah has targeted transgender people and those who host or organise around them. In October 2020 a coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups expressed concern over a probe of a Kedah event organiser for "encouraging vice" after a private birthday party was raided and 30 trans women were singled out and arrested. The pattern documented here is raid-based arrest and the punishment of organisers and allies, not individual stops of foreign visitors.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Kedah Sharia offences do not apply, but the federal Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the exposure that is documented is presence at a raided private event or venue, where arrest, public outing and prosecution under section 377B can follow.
tangentialFactors:
Kedah's section 26 is narrower than the cross-dressing provisions found elsewhere in Malaysia: it reaches only males posing as women in public, while three states also bar women from posing as men and Kedah does not. The penalties are lighter too, at up to RM1,000 or one year, against the three-year, RM5,000 and six-stroke ceiling that applies to the model provision across the other states and federal territories.

The October 2020 Kedah case extends exposure beyond the person who is trans. An organiser was investigated for "encouraging vice" over a private party at which 30 trans women were arrested, which places hosts, friends and service providers at risk of accessory-style liability under the same state regime.

The two layers move independently. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, while the federal Penal Code offences remained fully intact; whether those rulings bear on Kedah's 2014 enactment is not addressed in the sources available here.
localsOnly:
Muslim residents of Kedah face prosecution under sections 23, 24 and 26 of the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 for sodomy, lesbian sex and a male posing as a woman in public, with the fines, imprisonment and whipping set out above. Women convicted of musahaqah additionally face commitment to an approved home for up to six months under section 52, a measure that removes them from the community rather than merely penalising them.

Enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, and the cross-dressing offence contains no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. Residents therefore face liability defined by enforcement practice rather than by a statutory test.

Since the 1980s all 13 states have passed cross-dressing enactments, and government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021. LGBT events and media content are censored, there is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records enforcement activity under section 26 of the Kedah enactment after the October 2020 raid, so the current frequency of section 26 charges in Kedah is unresolved.

Whether the Federal Court's February 2021 and February 2024 federalism rulings apply to Kedah's 2014 enactment is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The inventory contains nothing on document or marker rules, entry and visa screening, bathroom or facilities rules, access to gender-affirming care, hate-crime protection, or partner recognition as they bear on Kedah; those items are not sourced rather than confirmed absent at state level.

The outcome of the probe into the Kedah event organiser opened in October 2020 is not stated in the source and is unresolved.
